vignette: The air still smells of cordite and burnt dust when Layla closes her eyes. It is not memory so much as presence, returning uninvited seven years after the convoy breaks apart under mortar fire. She is twenty-eight, twenty-nine, thirty-time fractures in the blast. One moment, she checks supply manifests in the cab of an armored transport; the next, the world turns white and loud. She tastes copper. She feels her body thrown against the steel door. She hears the sudden, absolute silence that follows the ringing. She survives. Others do not. The official report notes a mild traumatic brain injury and a fractured rib. The body remembers less. The nervous system remembers everything. When she returns home, Layla tries to fold herself back into the shape of a civilian wife. For three years, she walks through a house that feels too large, too quiet, too safe. She attempts to laugh at dinner, to plan vacations, to meet the expectations of a woman who is supposed to be healing. But safety feels like a performance. She flinches at car backfires in the driveway. She sleeps with the bedroom door locked, even though there is no one else in the house. Her husband stops asking where her mind goes. They stop speaking the same language. The divorce papers arrive in plain envelopes, not with anger, but with the quiet exhaustion of two people who can no longer occupy the same room. Her mother calls from Dubai, speaking in hushed tones about reputation and return, but Layla only nods, her throat tight, her attention fixed on the clock's ticking. She takes the principal position at Oakridge Middle School the following autumn. The building offers structure, predictable rhythms, children who need direction and will not ask for explanations she cannot give. She walks the halls with her shoulders rolled forward, her boots clicking a steady tempo against the linoleum. During budget meetings, she sits closest to the door, her notebook open, her pen moving continuously. She remembers every grant line, every parent complaint, every schedule change. She does not remember what the vice principal says three minutes ago. When the fire alarm tests on Thursdays, she is already in her car, hands on the wheel, breathing in measured counts until the silence returns. She avoids the faculty lounge. She eats lunch at her desk, alone. The weight of the badge she still keeps in her drawer feels heavier some days. Now, at thirty-eight, Layla arrives for our Tuesday afternoon sessions with a leather portfolio strapped across her chest. She unloads it methodically: attendance reports, discipline logs, emergency preparedness checklists. Her movements are precise, controlled, as if she is securing a perimeter. She tells me about the seventh-grade counselor who missed her shift, about the superintendent's question regarding enrollment declines, about the way the morning bell sounds too much like a radio burst. Her voice remains steady, but her right foot taps beneath the desk, a rapid, silent metronome. When I mention the sound of a dropped chair in the hallway outside, her pupils dilate. Her breath catches, just for a second, before she smooths her blazer and continues. She does not look at the window. She does not look at the clock. She looks at me, waiting for the conversation to stay exactly where she needs it to be: here, now, where nothing unexpected can catch her off guard.
